topic: sub:12|Relative frequency and probability|Multistage events, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B)

6086.stem: A pencil case contains 8 purple and 7 blue pens. Rebecca randomly selects 2 pens without replacement.

figures.cap: partial probability tree with first branches P and B
solution sketch: guideline's completed probability tree with PP and BB working

parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree diagram below to show Rebecca’s possible selections.

\exfigure{494_q12_1}
What is the probability that Rebecca selects two pens of the same colour?

criteria: Completes part of the tree, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Same colour means two blue or two purple.

$$\begin{aligned} P(BB \text{ or } PP) &= \dfrac{42}{210}+\dfrac{56}{210} \\ &= \dfrac{98}{210} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{15} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one correct probability of two pens of the same colour, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Criteria written by us. Added the intermediate fraction 98/210.

494_q12_1.notes: Partial tree left blank for students to complete: two straight 0.6pt branches from the root to P and B, with italic labels at the crop's positions. No probabilities are written because the crop has none. Rules 1, 3, 19, 21.

494_q12_s1.notes: Completed probability tree (P/B, then P/B) drawn with the house tree template (rule 21): horizontal, equal branch runs, symmetric fans, probabilities as stacked fractions (rule 23) centred above up-branches and below down-branches, outcome labels in one column per level. The teacher's PP and BB working (PP = 8/15 x 7/14 = 56/210, BB = 7/15 x 6/14 = 42/210) is typeset in the result column, level with the PP and BB outcomes. The low overlay score comes from the template layout (the crop's level-2 branches are shorter and uneven) and from typeset stacked fractions replacing the handwritten slashed ones; the overall size and layout match the crop.

6134.stem:
A bowl of fruit contains 21 pieces of fruit of which 8 are oranges and 13 are apples.

Jack takes one piece of fruit at random and eats it. Jill also takes a piece of fruit at random and eats it.

figures.cap: Blank probability tree: Jack (O, A) then Jill (O, A)
solution sketch: Completed probability tree with branch probabilities and outcomes OO, OA, AO, AA, as drawn in the guidelines

parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree diagram below by writing the probabilities on each branch.

\exfigure{720_q6_1}
Find the probability that Jack and Jill both ate an apple.
Find the probability that Jack and Jill ate different fruits.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{720_q6_s1}

First piece of fruit (21 pieces):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{8}{21}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{13}{21}$$
If Jack ate an orange, 20 pieces remain (7 oranges, 13 apples):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{7}{20}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{13}{20}$$
If Jack ate an apple, 20 pieces remain (8 oranges, 12 apples):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{8}{20}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{12}{20}$$
criteria: Completes first branch, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Both ate an apple, so multiply along the apple-apple branches.
$$\begin{aligned} P(AA) &= \dfrac{13}{21} \times \dfrac{12}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{35} \end{aligned}$$

Different fruits means orange then apple, or apple then orange. Add the two branch products.
$$\begin{aligned} P(OA \text{ or } AO) &= \dfrac{8}{21} \times \dfrac{13}{20} + \dfrac{13}{21} \times \dfrac{8}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{52}{105} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One correct multiplication for either $OA$ or $AO$, or equivalent merit

720_q6_1.notes: Blank tree built with the house template (rule 21): horizontal, equal branch run, level-2 fans symmetric with equal gaps. The crop's fans are uneven (upper fan -135/+100 px, lower -83/+132 px), which explains the low overlay. Level 1 matches the crop. O and A are in maths italic (rule 19). The Jack and Jill headings sit over the branch midpoints as in the crop. No probabilities, because this is the question figure.

720_q6_s1.notes: Solution tree built with the house template (rule 21). Probabilities are stacked \dfrac (rule 23): 8/21 and 13/21, 7/20 and 13/20, 8/20 and 12/20, each above an up-branch and below a down-branch. The handwritten pink 'Outcomes' column (OO, OA, AO, AA) is redrawn in black maths italic (rules 6, 19). Round 2 widened the level-1 fan so the OA and AO rows and the 13/20 and 8/20 labels have clear room. Overlay is low because the crop is handwritten and its fans are uneven; the structure and labels match.

6379.stem:
There are three candidates for team leader on a camp, Andie, Bec and Cat.

There are two candidates for team mascot at the camp, Miao and Woof.

Based on a survey of camp attendees, the probability tree shows the likelihood of the candidates being chosen for each position.

\exfigure{308_q19_1}

figures.cap: probability tree: leader A, B, C then mascot M, W

parts.latex: What is the probability that Andie will be leader with Miao as mascot?
What is the probability that Andie will be the leader or Miao will be the mascot, but not both?

solutions.latex:
Multiply along the branches $A$ then $M$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A \text{ and } M) &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

"Andie or Miao but not both" means either (Andie and Woof) or (not Andie and Miao).

Andie and Woof:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} &= \dfrac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Bec or Cat, with Miao:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{6}\right) \times \dfrac{1}{3} &= \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Add the two cases:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{2}{9} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one of the two required probabilities correctly, or equivalent merit

308_q19_1.notes: Built with the house tree template (rule 21), with treeL set to 4cm to match the crop's branch run. Root to A/B/C (1/3, 1/2, 1/6), then each to M (1/3) and W (2/3). Vertical spacing matches the crop (A/C at ±3.6cm, children at ±0.9cm). Probabilities are \dfrac (rule 23). Each W probability now sits below its downward branch, where the paper wrote it between the two branches (rule 21). The low overlay comes from the template's fonts, label column and probability placement, not from errors in the geometry. Check this one first.

6434.stem: 45% of the residents in a local community have been administered only one vaccination against a spreading virus and 30% of the residents have been administered two vaccinations (so that they are fully vaccinated).

parts.latex: What is the probability that a randomly chosen resident from the community has NOT been administered at least ONE vaccination?
If TWO residents are randomly selected from the community, what is the probability that at least ONE of them has been administered at least ONE vaccination?

solutions.latex:
The probability of no vaccination is one minus the probability of one or two vaccinations.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.45+0.3) \\ &= 0.25 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 25\% \text{ or } 0.25 \text{ or } \dfrac{1}{4}$$

Use the complement: at least one vaccinated is one minus neither vaccinated.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.25\times 0.25) \\ &= 1-0.0625 \\ &= 0.9375 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 0.9375 \text{ or } 93.75\%$$
criteria: Uses the complement, or equivalent merit

6514.stem:
There are two bags of lollies. One bag has three green frogs and two red frogs, while the second bag has four green frogs and five red frogs.

One bag is chosen at random, and two frogs are picked from the bag, without replacement.

figures.cap: partly completed two-stage tree diagram for two bags

parts.latex:
Complete the below tree diagram below by writing probabilities in the boxes.

\exfigure{1266_q36_1}
Calculate the probability of picking two red frogs.
Calculate the probability of picking at least one green frog.

criteria: Completes at least one pair of branches correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Each bag is chosen with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$; then two reds are drawn without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{two red}) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{5}{9} \times \dfrac{4}{8} \\ &= \dfrac{17}{90} \\ &\approx 18.9\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to calculate the probability, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the complementary event.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one green}) &= 1 - P(\text{two red}) \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{17}{90} \\ &= \dfrac{73}{90} \\ &\approx 81.1\% \end{aligned}$$

1266_q36_1.notes: Built on the tree template (rule 21) with treeL=2.8cm. Probabilities are framed boxes, all the same size; the boxes to fill in are empty, with 1/2, 4/9, 5/9, 1/4, 3/8, 5/8, 4/8, 4/8 as on the paper. The low overlay score is expected because the template fans the branches symmetrically. DEFECT: in round 2 the inner level-2 gap became too small, so the 1/4 box (below Bag1-R-R) touches the 3/8 box (above Bag2-G-G). Fix: change the level-2 y values from +/-40pt to about +/-50pt (or level 1 from +/-85pt to about +/-95pt). I stopped here because of the 2-round limit.

1266_q36_s1.notes: Completed tree on the same template and geometry as q36_1: 1/2,1/2; 3/5,2/5; 4/9,5/9; 2/4,2/4; 3/4,1/4; 3/8,5/8; 4/8,4/8, all in framed boxes of one size. The low score is expected because the template spaces branches evenly. DEFECT: as in q36_1, the 1/4 and 3/8 boxes touch in the middle. The same fix applies (widen the level-2 inner gap to about +/-50pt). Not re-rendered because of the 2-round limit.
